---
title: "Sound 7: FM Synthesis"
toc: true
toc-depth: 2

**FM** (frequency modulation) synthesis makes harmonics by a different route from
[subtractive synthesis](sound-subtractive.qmd). Instead of starting rich and filtering, it starts with
two plain sine waves and uses one to wobble the pitch of the other so fast that the wobble becomes
new frequencies. John Chowning found this at Stanford in 1967; Yamaha built it into the DX7 in 1983,
and its electric piano, bells and slap bass are all over the music of the 1980s.

**How to use the page.** Press **▶ Demo** or play the keys or MIDI. Choose a preset, then change one
control at a time. The dashed lines on the spectrum mark where FM puts its new frequencies.

## Carrier and modulator

<div class="sk" data-w="fm" data-preset="Steady (to study)"></div>

- The **carrier** is the sine wave you hear. Its frequency is the note you play.
- The **modulator** is a second sine wave that you don't hear directly. It moves the carrier's pitch
  up and down.
- The **ratio** is the modulator's frequency divided by the carrier's.
- The **index** is how far the modulator pushes the pitch. At 0 there's no modulation: a plain sine.

This is the vibrato from the [LFO lesson](sound-lfo.qmd), sped up into the audio range. Below about
20 Hz you hear a wobble; above it you hear a new *timbre*.

## Sidebands

With the preset **Steady (to study)** loaded, hold a note and slowly raise the **index** from 0.
New spikes appear on the spectrum on both sides of the carrier, spaced by the modulator's frequency:
carrier ± 1 × modulator, ± 2 ×, ± 3 × and so on. These are **sidebands**. The higher the index, the
more sidebands, and the brighter the sound.

Now change the **ratio**:

- **Whole-number ratios** (1, 2, 3…) put every sideband on a harmonic of the note. The sound is
  pitched and "musical". Ratio 1 gives every harmonic, like a sawtooth; ratio 2 gives only odd
  harmonics, like a square or a clarinet.
- **Other ratios** (1.41, 3.5…) put the sidebands between harmonics. The sound is
  **inharmonic**: metallic, bell-like, clangorous. That's how FM makes bells and gongs so easily,
  which subtractive synths find hard.
- **Modulator fine tune** detunes the modulator a few cents: the sidebands beat against each other and
  the sound shimmers.

## Envelopes make FM come alive

In FM the **index** does the job of the filter in a subtractive synth: it sets the brightness. Give
the index its own envelope and the brightness changes during each note, the way real instruments do.

- **Bell**: index starts high and dies away, the volume dies away more slowly. The clang at the
  start fades into a pure hum.
- **Electric piano**: ratio 1, a quick index decay: a bright "tine" attack and a mellow body.
- **Brass**: the index rises with the attack, so the note gets brighter as it swells.
- **Bass**: a short burst of index gives the slap at the start of each note.

Try the **Bell** preset and change only the ratio: 3.5, 1.4, 2.76, 5.19. Each is a different metal.

## FM and the spectrum, in one sentence

Subtractive starts with all the harmonics and removes some; additive ([Sound 1](sound-harmonics.qmd))
sets each harmonic by hand; FM makes a whole family of frequencies from two sine waves, controlled by
just two numbers: the ratio decides *where* they go and the index decides *how many*.
